title: Where Language Falters

opening: There's a difference between knowing that everything dies and actually living with that knowledge.

fragment: We all know that we are mortal, yet much of our everyday lives unfold as though we weren't.

We make plans, form attachments, and establish routines with an unspoken expectation of continuity. And perhaps this is necessary, for how could we live if we carried the full weight of impermanence in every waking moment?
Yet to truly recognize mortality is not necessarily to become pessimistic or detached.
It is simply to understand that death is not an exception to life, nor something that goes wrong with existence. It is part of what existence is.
Still, accepting mortality intellectually does not free us from our emotional attachment to particular lives.
We may understand that everything must eventually end, yet find ourselves wishing for another day, another year, another moment with those we love.
And perhaps this is where the bittersweetness of life resides: between our capacity to recognize impermanence and our equally profound capacity to love what is impermanent.

closing: Knowing that everything ends does not make what happens before the ending any less real.
